text:
He said that he had thought about himself and about her—about her above all—and had understood that they were both preparing, with their own hands, an irreparable ruin. That she was young and had to live, while he would never have consented to share her with anyone. And she must let no illusion blind her. Today, perhaps, her greatest joy lay in sacrificing herself, but inevitably a day would come, and perhaps not a distant one, when she would repent of it too late. Indeed, how many aspirations, how many impatient longings were already tormenting her ardent youth! For she was a child of twenty, and at twenty love, even so troubled a love, can be nothing but a gust of sentiment, a breath of perverse ardor, which fades and passes and leaves no memory of itself... Then, in the long run, nothing can be hidden. People, sooner or later, would notice. And then?... Did she feel she had the courage to endure such shame openly? Everyone would execrate them, shun them like two leprous dogs, like two creatures possessed, and for them there would remain neither family, nor friends, nor future, nor peace, nor any of those human comforts that are, after all, necessary to every creature. Moreover, they were not rich, and it was therefore necessary that each, along a separate path, provide for the future, since both had chosen a road different from the one marked out in their destiny. If they had been rich, perhaps, very rich, they could have fled to a country where no one knew them or could ever come to know them, and there forget that they had been born of the same mother, the same father, remembering only that they loved one another.

But even if that were so, would they ever have found peace in their own consciences? “Remember!—he said to her—everything can be silenced except the inexorable voice that rises from the depths of our heart. And remorse, you see, is the most terrible enemy of all those life holds in store for us.”

And not only that: but what if a child were born of their sin? What if they should ever give the world a creature so accursed from its very origin? What if from the two of them, brother and sister, there should be born an infamous creature, excluded from all human laws, who would make them tremble whenever its childish mouth uttered those first words that are babbled: “mamma, papa...”

Had she ever thought of all this? Certainly not; because she was still young, inexperienced in every danger, and let herself be seized unthinkingly by the madness of her love, which was only “her first love...”

For him too it was the first, the only, truly the one and only. And she would certainly recover from it; he would not. He would do everything possible to forget, but all this would serve only to mingle his poisonous malady more deeply into his veins. For her, without a doubt, it was nothing but a slight caprice, a gust of wind, an impetuous wave of heat in the freshness of her twenty years... Oh, she must not say no! He knew it well, and this was perhaps his greatest torment. But he, on the other hand, was already a mature man and, indeed, a man who until then had remained insensible to every passion; and so a dark storm had been unleashed in his soul, one of those storms that overwhelm and destroy an entire life. However much he struggled with all his strength, there was now no escape; another man had suddenly entered into him, utterly different from the man he had been until then; his mind, his heart, his senses—everything had changed. His free youth had been chained on the day he had begun to love her, and now he lived as though under the magic of a spell; he no longer knew how to master himself; he was beside himself.

He had to arm himself with all his strength so as not to drag her too into his own ruin; he had to love her with an infinite love, more than love, with a boundless adoration, in order to come and tell her what he was telling her:

—“I am leaving, I am fleeing; you will never see me again. I must stay far from you even if it kills me; I must renounce you so that you may be happy later. I must find within my human strength the pitiless strength not to take you, and to go away, alone, to seek refuge who knows where—I who love you, I who do not live a single moment without thinking of you, I who, wherever I go, shall carry in my senses and in my soul the memory of you, more vivid and more terrible than you yourself... And that is not all. You are defended, watched over; there is your father, our father, who defends you. Every time my lips wished to kiss you, I would see him now. Last night, when we were together, when you were almost mine, all at once he came; I saw him. He was there, between you and me, looking at me with his unwavering eyes. His face merged with your face. I heard our father cursing us. And now his specter no longer leaves me. Do you understand, Loretta, do you understand that it would drive me mad?...

“I ask only one thing of you: have pity on me. Do nothing to keep me here; do not weep; do not repeat that you would have wished to be mine. Instead you must hate me, because this love I have for you—remember!—is a horrible thing. Do as you wish: go back home, or stay, or go wherever you will be happy. But do not forget that a man is fleeing, casting his dead heart out of life, to save you, solely to save from ruin the sister whom he loved...

“Later, when you are a woman, remember that if my guilt was great, I also struggled as much as a man can struggle to rebel against this guilt. And do not say anything to me, Lora... never seek me again. I am leaving at once, this morning, in an hour...”


And he left.




                   *       *       *       *       *




I


She remained in that hotel for two days, lost, inert, astonished, bewildered. What was happening was new, unexpected, to her. The revelation of this desperate love, the tragic aspect of this passion, at first gave her a sense of painful wonder.

She did not understand love in this way; for her, love could be nothing but a romantic tangle of sad and joyful sensations, of words that come to the lips to be transformed into a kiss, of unsatisfied curiosities, of vehement aspirations toward a physical contentment unknown to her. For her, then, love was meant to be a joyous thing.

She was nothing but a little wasp, light, fickle, stinging: she felt a sense of unease before this love so tragic. She had become enamored of her brother, but without finding in it the slightest savor of incest; indeed, she had loved him by instinct, without thinking of his name, without even realizing that she was violating a sacred prohibition. She had met him when, in her voluptuous lover’s womb, still sealed, she felt an invincible need for self-surrender, wrapped in the obscure lusts that torment the fire of virginity. From him she had undergone her first temptation; for him she had felt the first dark unrest of love arise in her blood; her virgin womb, thus and in no other way, loved him.

She was at once so simple and so perverse that she could feel an incestuous love purely; the evil lay so well hidden within her that she did not know she was contaminated by it.

Man, who in his actions is often impulsive, nevertheless loves to question himself, to debate his own passions; woman, who by nature instead has a reflective spirit, when a strong passion binds her, debates no longer and allows her desire to surrender itself to it without a shadow of fear. Nothing is so pleasing to her as escaping the dominion of her own will, whereas it is always with great regret that we relinquish power over ourselves.
